parts.title: Using computer models that learn from their own past predictions to forecast how many hospital beds will be in use
parts.abstract:
Background

A hospital keeps its costs down only if it plans well how many beds it needs. In this work we tackle the problem of predicting how many beds will be in use several months ahead. We focus on one use case: planning when doctors, nurses and other staff take their holidays.

Methods

We built a model from a set of recursive neural networks. A neural network is a computer program that learns patterns from examples. "Recursive" means it feeds its own prediction for one day into itself to make the prediction for the next day. Our model predicts bed use by combining past records of patients arriving and leaving with outside information such as public holidays and school holidays. It needs no personal information about patients or staff. We tuned it to make 60-day forecasts during the summer season (May to September).

Results

We tested the model on 8 separate sets of data that it had not learned from. On average, its mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was 6.24%. MAPE measures how far off the predictions are, on average, as a percentage of the real number of beds in use.

Conclusions

Our machine learning model holds up well against standard forecasting methods that work with data recorded over time. We recommend it for use in the automatic scheduling and decision-making systems of medium-sized hospitals.
parts.introduction_first: Hospitals forecast how many beds will be in use mainly because they need to make the best use of their resources. This need is widely understood, and it keeps growing as medical care becomes more and more competitive [1, 2]. The better our predictions, the further ahead we can plan. As a result, resources are used more efficiently, and patients can receive better care [3–5].
parts.conclusion:
Conclusions

We presented a mathematical model built on recurrent artificial neural networks, designed to forecast how many beds will be in use in hospitals. Recurrent NARX networks are a type of neural network that learns from its own past predictions as well as from outside information. They have already been used successfully to model data recorded over time in other fields. As far as we know, though, this is the first time NARX has been used to plan hospital beds.

Our model reached a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 6.24% on 60-day forecasts. That puts it on a par with the best methods available today, and it does so without any personal information about patients. Instead, it relies only on records of patients arriving and leaving. We tuned the model for the summer season, using data from a medium-sized German hospital, with the goal of better scheduling.

The model is flexible and can easily be adapted to different needs. In particular, it can be built into an automatic decision-making system, for example one like the one developed by Grübler and colleagues [40]. We are now developing a web-based application that anyone can use for free. It will have an easy-to-use interface and will run faster.
parts.introduction_rest:
Forecasting how many beds will be in use can be done at many different scales and from many different points of view. At one end, a country may want to plan its hospitals and their buildings. That is a very large area and a very long stretch of time. In the middle, a hospital needs to plan when its staff take their holidays, weeks or months ahead, so that the hospital keeps running smoothly even though the number of patients rises and falls with the seasons. At the other end, we might ask about a single department in a local hospital, hour by hour. For example, this could help plan the short term in an emergency department or an intensive care unit (ICU), where seriously ill patients are treated. Which methods work best depends a great deal on the situation and on how the problem is set up.

In recent years, most research has built mathematical forecasting models for ICUs. The risk of a disruption to patient care is especially high there, and the time scale is very short, sometimes just minutes [6–9]. On the other hand, the large money costs involved push hospitals to forecast bed use further ahead, for medium to long-term planning, that is, weeks, months or years [10–14].

In this paper, we look at forecasting bed use over a medium stretch of time, a few months ahead, for medium-sized hospitals with 250 to 500 beds. Our data are recorded once a day. We assume that patterns that repeat over time, such as weekly, seasonal and yearly changes, play a key role in the model. Being able to forecast bed use, and so how staff and other resources will be used, several months ahead makes it easier to plan where people work. This matters most during public holidays, school holidays and other periods of interest.

There is fairly little information about how others have solved problems like ours. Mackay and colleagues give a broad overview of existing models for forecasting in hospitals, from very simple ones to more modern and complex ones [15]. Many of these models rely on estimates of the length of stay, meaning how long a patient stays in hospital [16, 17]. Here, instead, we present a more direct approach that works with data recorded over time. It needs only past records of patients arriving and leaving, and no personal information about patients.

One of the first times methods for data recorded over time were used for the problem of bed use was a study by Farmer and colleagues [10]. They suggested a stochastic approach, one that takes the random ups and downs in the data into account. They used a method called ARIMA (short for autoregressive integrated moving average), together with a step-by-step procedure for choosing its settings known as the Box-Jenkins method [18]. ARIMA models predict the next value from past values and from the errors of earlier predictions. This family of models has a long history of use in business, for example in simulating the stock market [19], and it rests on a solid mathematical foundation [20].

In recent decades, methods that learn from data, and machine learning in particular, have proved very effective at forecasting [21–23]. However, only limited progress has been made in using them to forecast how many beds will be in use. Researchers have built machine learning models that forecast the length of stay [16, 24–27], when patients are discharged [28] and when they are readmitted to hospital [29]. Joy and Jones [30] proposed combining ARIMA with artificial neural networks to model bed use over time. In their approach, though, the neural network part only estimates the leftover errors that ARIMA misses.

As far as we know, when we submitted this paper, no scientific work was available that describes a machine learning model as the main tool for forecasting bed use from data recorded over time.

Our main goal is to build a computer model that takes past records of patients arriving and leaving each day, combines them with outside information that anyone can find publicly, and gives a forecast for a future period. We explore the advantages of recurrent neural networks, which feed their own past predictions into themselves, and we show that they can be used successfully to forecast how many beds will be in use over a medium stretch of time.
parts.results:
## Results

### Finding the best settings

We first looked for the settings that gave the best forecasts. We judged them over a 60-day forecast period, starting on the first day of each summer month from May to August in the years 2009 to 2013. Three settings mattered most. The first was how many days of past data the model learned from before it started making forecasts. We call this the training length. The second was the delay, which is how many days back the model looks when it makes a prediction. The third was the network's inner structure.

The best results came from a training length of 1 year (k = 365 days), a delay of 2 days (d = 2), and a network with two hidden layers, each holding two nodes (Table 1). Hidden layers are the inner layers of a neural network, and nodes are the small calculating units inside them. With these settings, the model's mean absolute error (MAE) was 12.1 beds. MAE is the average size of the gap between the predicted and the real number of beds in use, in beds rather than as a percentage.

We also checked whether the model did better on some days of the week than others. The differences between days of the week were not statistically significant. This means we could not show a real difference between them. It does not prove that there is none.

We also tried letting the model learn from longer stretches of past data. None of these gave a better result (Table 1).

Next, we asked how far ahead the model could look. When it forecast a whole year (365 days), its average MAE was 15.65 beds, give or take 2.65 beds (Table 2). The "give or take" figure is the standard deviation, which shows how much the results spread out around the average. When we used the best settings on the summer months of the data we had set aside for testing, the average MAE was 12.51 beds, give or take 2.54 beds (Table 3).

The results showed that only 1 year of past data worked best. That raised a natural question. What if we simply forecast the same number of beds that were needed on the same day last year? To test this idea, we built a naive model. It predicts exactly the same number of beds as 1 year ago.

The day of the week is an important sign of how many beds are in use (Fig. 4). So instead of looking back 365 days, the naive model looked back 364 days. That way, the day of the week stays the same.

The naive model's average MAE was 16.4 beds, give or take 2.9 beds. It did better than our NARX model only in one of the eight forecasts (Fig. 5).

Fig. 4

An example of a 60-day forecast starting in May 2014, showing the predicted and the real number of beds in use

Fig. 5

The MAE of the NARX model compared with the naive model for the summer seasons of 2014–2015

We also wanted to compare our work with the work of Kim and colleagues [11]. For this, we worked out the MAPE for forecasts 1 day and 30 days ahead. For the 1-day forecast, we predicted each day in the summer period from May to August 2014 to 2015 on its own. For the 30-day forecast, we predicted the first 30 days of each summer month from May to August 2014 to 2015.

The MAPE was 4.01% (give or take 3.16%) for the 1-day forecast. For the 30-day forecast, it was 5.55% (give or take 1.21%).
parts.methods:
## Methods

Our aim was to forecast how many beds will be in use in a hospital. To do this, we built a model based on recurrent neural networks. We tuned the model mainly for one task: planning when medical staff work, so that the hospital can cope with the rise and fall of patient numbers through the seasons.

The model is based on a real situation. In it, several clinics share a pool of beds, counted in groups of 30 beds. Each group of 30 is called a unit. A unit can be closed or opened depending on how many beds are in use at the moment. Each unit also needs its own staff. So, in practice, the real goal of the forecast is to estimate correctly how many units will be needed at any point in time.

People from hospital management asked for a reliable prediction of bed use 60 days ahead. The forecasts should start on the first day of each of the main holiday months: May, June, July and August.

### The data we used

Our work is based on the records of a medium-sized German hospital with about 400 beds. The records cover the period from 14 October 2002 to 31 December 2015, which is 4827 days. Each record lists a patient's ID number, the date the patient arrived and the date the patient left, and the name of the clinic the patient was admitted to. No personal information about patients or staff was included. In total, 353,520 records were available. A separate list names the clinics that share their beds.

### Cleaning, preparing and adding extra information

We prepared the data in 5 steps: (1) cleaning it by removing missing values, (2) cleaning it by removing data we did not need, (3) turning it into a form we could use, (4) adding outside information, and (5) splitting it into data for learning, data for testing and data for the final check.

#### Cleaning the data

In step 1, we removed every record that had a missing value, such as a missing date or patient number. These made up about 2% of all the data, so removing them would not really affect the model.

In step 2, we removed data from clinics that were not part of the shared bed pool. These were intensive care units (ICUs) and specialty clinics that did not share their beds. They made up about 50% of all the data.

#### Turning the data into a daily count

Step 3 was needed because the original records do not directly tell us how many beds were in use on each day. Instead, they give the arrival and departure times of individual patients. To build a daily record of bed use, we first need to know how many beds were in use on the very first day. Since this number was not available, we assumed it was zero.

To make up for this mistake, we threw away the first 168 days of the daily record. That is the same as throwing away everything before 1 April 2003. We only used patients with a complete record, meaning both an arrival date and a departure date. So patients who arrived before 14 October 2002 are not part of the daily record. By the date we chose, 1 April 2003, their number is small enough to ignore (Fig. 1).

The result of this step is a single daily record of bed use, from 1 April 2003 to 31 December 2015. It is a list of 4657 numbers, one for each day.

Fig. 1

Bed use over the whole period covered by the data, showing only the shared beds. Bed use builds up in the first days (pink background) and becomes steady by April 2003. In 2005, the clinics reorganized their beds, which shows up as a drop in the number of beds in use (red bar/line). Yellow background marks the data used for learning and testing, and green background marks the data used for the final check.

#### Adding outside information

In step 4, we added outside information that is likely to affect how many beds are in use. After talking with the hospital managers, we added the following:

Day of the week. We coded the days as numbers from 1 to 7, from Monday to Sunday. This helps the model learn the weekly pattern, such as more patients arriving at weekends.

Day of the year. We coded the days as numbers from 1 to 365 or 366, from 1 January to 31 December. This shows the time of year.

Public holidays. For each date, this is a simple yes-or-no answer: is it a public holiday or not? The hospital lies on the border of three German federal states, and some German holidays are set by each state. So we added one yes-or-no record for each state.

School holidays. We coded these in the same way as public holidays, with three separate yes-or-no records, one for each state.

We took the holiday information from the website of the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs (Kultusministerkonferenz), the organization that publishes school holidays in Germany [31].

We arranged all the outside information (day of the week, day of the year, national and school holidays, and information from both the past and the future) into a set of records over time, lined up with the daily record of bed use. It forms a table with 9 rows and 4657 columns, one column for each day from 1 April 2003 to 31 December 2015 (Fig. 2).

Fig. 2

The 9 pieces of outside information for each day. S1, S2 and S3 stand for three German federal states. Pink, yellow and green show the build-up, learning and final-check data, matching the phases in Fig. 1.

The final data set for building the model therefore contains the daily bed use together with the outside information about conditions. When forecasting, the outside information can be known for future days, but the bed use can only be known for days that have already passed.

#### Splitting the data into learning, testing and final-check data

We divided the cleaned data into two parts. The first part, used for learning and testing, covers 1 April 2003 to 31 December 2013. We used it to tune the model's settings. The second part, from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, is used only for the final check. We used it just once, to see how well the model predicts data it has never seen.

We split the learning and testing data into separate blocks, called folds. Each month from May to August in the years 2009 to 2013 served as a test period, giving 20 test cases in total. For each test case, the model learned from the 1 to 5 years before that date.

### The NARX model

Machine learning methods such as artificial neural networks, decision trees and support vector machines have been used successfully in engineering and business (see [21] for an overview). They are still rarely mentioned when it comes to forecasting for hospital management.

Several studies also compare NARX with standard forecasting methods that work with data recorded over time. These methods are autoregressive-moving-average (ARMA), autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA), seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA) and generalized autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity (GARCH) [32].

It is hard to draw general conclusions. Still, comparisons based on particular data, such as laser measurements that behave in a chaotic way [33], wind speed [34] or the production of refrigeration compressors [35], tend to agree that NARX works better than these standard methods, especially when forecasting several steps ahead [33].

The NARX model assumes that the value we want to predict, here the number of beds in use (written y), at a given time t depends on two things. The first is the recent past of that same value: the last d_y days. The second is the outside information at that time: a set of 8 values (written u) covering the last d_u days:

(1) y(t) = f(y(t−1), y(t−2), …, y(t−d_y), u(t−1), u(t−2), …, u(t−d_u))

In words, the model predicts today's bed use from the bed use of the last few days and from the outside information of the last few days.

The lengths of this memory, d_y and d_u, affect how complicated the model is and how long it takes to compute. To keep things simple, we assume d_y = d_u = d. We call d the "delay". We choose its value while tuning the model.

Equation (1) captures the core idea of the model we propose. Besides the delay d, we need several more settings to describe the function f. Here, f is a neural network with h_L hidden layers and a fixed number h_N of nodes (small calculating units) in each layer. During forecasting, the network becomes recursive: its prediction for y(t) becomes an input for the next step. That is why it is called a recurrent neural network.

### Learning and testing the NARX model

To organize the work, we set out a four-step procedure for learning and testing the model. We use it again and again to tune the model's settings and to forecast future bed use. Only afterwards do we judge the overall performance using the final-check data.

During learning, the NARX model runs in what is called an open loop. During testing, it runs in a closed loop. In the open loop, all the information comes from the outside information. In the closed loop, part of the data is fed back from the network to itself (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3

Open-loop learning and closed-loop prediction of NARX, shown on an example of bed use data with a delay d = 2. Prediction and learning are handled the same way for the learning data and the final-check data. To keep things simple, the outside information is not shown. It always comes from the already-calculated daily records (top bar) and never from the predictions.

Here is an example. Suppose we use a history of 1 year and a delay of 2 to predict 60 days starting on 1 May 2008. The learning data would be the 365 days before 1 May 2008, which, because 2008 is a leap year, runs from 2 May 2007 to 30 April 2008.

To predict the first day (1 May 2008), the NARX model uses the bed use of 29 and 30 April 2008. To predict the second day (2 May 2008), it uses the first prediction (1 May 2008) and the bed use on the last day of April. From then on, it uses only the newly predicted bed numbers (closed loop).

#### Step 1: Fix the model settings

We choose the first day of the 60-day forecast period.

In the daily record, this day is a certain day number t_0, and t_0 − d must fall within the period covered by the data. The following settings must be fixed before learning:

delay d = d_y = d_u (see eq. (1)): the delay of the model. It says how many days in the past are assumed to affect day t_0.

history k: the length of history used for learning. In other words, we use a k-year stretch of the data (for example, the last year) instead of all earlier data.

h_L: the number of hidden layers.

h_N: the number of nodes in each hidden layer.

#### Step 2: Learning the model

To learn, the NARX model needs the data for each learning round chosen (see Fig. 3). For each date t_i between t_0 − k and t_0 − 1, we pair the input (y(t_i − d), …, y(t_i − 1), u(t_i − d), …, u(t_i)) with the output y(t_i). Because t_0 − 1 must be in the data and is the last day of the learning data, the real bed numbers y are known for every day in the learning data.

The neural network learns using a method called backpropagation. It compares its prediction with the real value, works out how wrong it was, and then adjusts its internal settings a little to reduce that mistake. It repeats this many times.

#### Step 3: Forecasting and testing the model

We use the learned NARX model to forecast a 60-day period (t_0 to t_0 + 60) (see Fig. 3). This has to be done step by step, because whatever t_0 we choose, we assume the future bed numbers y(t_0), …, y(t_0 + 60) are unknown. The outside information u, on the other hand, is available for every day, including future days.

In the first step, we give the model the input (y(t_0 − d), …, y(t_0 − 1), u(t_0 − d), …, u(t_0)). It gives an output ŷ(t_0), where the hat means "predicted". This prediction becomes the input for the next step. After repeating this 60 times, we have the 60-day forecast ŷ(t_0), …, ŷ(t_0 + 60 − 1).

#### Step 4: Making the results more reliable

The backpropagation method we use starts from random values for the NARX model's settings and improves them step by step during learning. Because of this, the predictions could vary a lot. One way to prevent this would be to fix the random starting point, called the seed, so that the results could be fully repeated. On the other hand, some seeds can also lead to very large errors.

To make the predictions steadier without losing the benefit of the random starting point, we decided to repeat steps 2 and 3 many times (here 50 times) and average the results. This makes the computing time grow in step with the number of repeats, but it makes the results more reliable.

### Measuring errors

There are several ways to judge how good a forecast is. Usually, the error on each day is written e_i = |y(t_i) − ŷ(t_i)|, for t_i from t_0 to t_0 + 60 − 1. Here y is the real number of beds in use and ŷ is the predicted number. The vertical bars mean we take the size of the difference, ignoring whether the prediction was too high or too low.

In this work, we chose the following measures:

MAX = max(|e_i|, i = 1..60). The maximum error tells us about the worst prediction in the 60-day forecast period.

MAE = mean(|e_i|, i = 1..60). The mean absolute error gives an overall picture of how good the forecast is.

MAPE = 100 × mean(|e_i/y_i|, i = 1..60). The mean absolute percentage error shows the average error as a percentage of the real number of beds. It is often used in similar problems [11], which makes comparisons easier.

RMSE = √(1/n ∑_{i=1}^{60} e_i²). The root-mean-square error is a kind of average that gives extra weight to large mistakes. Like MAPE, it makes comparisons easier.

GE = max(floor(ŷ/30 + 1) − floor(y/30 + 1)), i = 1..60. This measure is special to our problem. As we mentioned earlier, clinics share beds in groups of 30. So it is important that, over the forecast period, the number of groups actually needed stays as close as possible to the number predicted. Even a forecast that is good on average can count as a failure if it is badly wrong on just one day. GE can take the values one and zero. It captures the largest difference between the number of units actually needed and the number predicted, whether the forecast was too many or too few. Any positive number means that, on at least 1 day during the forecast period, either one or more units were empty or too few beds were available.

From here on, we use the mean absolute error (MAE) as the main guide when tuning the model. Unlike the maximum error, MAE is not thrown off by a single day's ups and downs. It is also less sensitive to small changes than GE, which is based on a threshold: a difference of just one bed can make a big difference.

Compared with MAPE and RMSE, MAE is easier to understand, while it is similar in most other ways. Later, we will see that, despite these small differences, all four kinds of error show the same overall picture.

### Tuning the model's settings

Our current model has four settings that we can choose: k, h_L, h_N and d (described in Step 1 and 4 above). Finding the best combination of all of them would take a very large amount of computing. Finding a good combination close to the best one, called a local optimum, could be done fairly quickly. To do this, we used the following procedure.

#### Tuning the learning history k and the number of hidden nodes h_N

We assume the other settings are h_L = 1 and d = 2. For every pair of values h_N ∈ {1, 5, 10, 15, …, 40} and k ∈ {365, 730, 1095, 1460, 1825} (1 to 5 years), we run the basic forecasting procedure for the dates 1 May, June, July and August in 2009–2013.

For each date, value of k and value of h_N, we calculate the five kinds of error described above.

For each fixed pair (k, h_N), we average the errors over the dates.

We choose the best pair (k_0, h_N_0) as the one with the smallest mean absolute error (MAE).

#### Tuning the number of hidden layers h_L

For (k_0, h_N_0), we check the results for different numbers of layers (h_L) and fix the best value h_L_0.

#### Tuning the delay d, the recent past used for prediction

For (k_0, h_N_0, h_L_0), we tune the last setting, d.

We repeat this whole process. The settings found in one round become the starting settings for the next round, until the settings stop changing from one round to the next. In this way, we found a local optimum for the model's settings.

### Checking the model

For the best settings we had chosen, we run the basic forecasting procedure on the summer seasons of 2014 and 2015. We make 60-day forecasts starting on 1 May, June, July and August, and calculate the five kinds of error. Finally, we make full forecasts for the whole year, starting on 1 January, for the years 2009–2015. This shows how well the model carries over to different conditions, such as the sudden changes around the major holidays.

### Software

We did the calculations in MATLAB R2017a (The Mathworks, Natick, MA, USA). We built the NARX model with the Neural Network Toolbox.
parts.discussion:
Discussion

Many hospitals predict how many beds will be in use by looking at how long each patient stays in hospital. This is called the length of stay. To make such a prediction, they use information about each patient, such as their age, gender, medical history or the results of medical tests [26]. Our approach works differently. It predicts bed use from data recorded over time, and it needs no personal information about any patient, no details about hospital staff and no records of the medical procedures carried out. This means it can be considered privacy preserving.

Even so, it is not easy to compare our approach directly with earlier work. There is also no public collection of data that others have used to test their methods, so the comparisons we make can only give a rough idea of how well each method performs. To judge the methods fairly, all of them should be tested on the same set of data.

Kim and colleagues [11] compared a simple method, which just averages past values, with several standard methods for data recorded over time. These are called ARIMA, SARIMA and GARCH. They report a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 6% for forecasts 1 day ahead and 8.8% for forecasts 30 days ahead. On our test data, the average MAPE was 4.01% for 1-day forecasts, 5.55% for 30-day forecasts and 5.48% for 60-day forecasts. This suggests that our NARX model performs better than the traditional methods for data recorded over time.

Jones and colleagues [36] report a root mean square error (RMSE) of about 15 beds over a 32-day forecast period. RMSE is another way of measuring the typical size of a prediction error, and it gives extra weight to large mistakes. In their case, the average number of beds in use was about 440. Our model reached an RMSE of 14.99 for 60-day forecasts and 13.51 for 30-day forecasts, with about 220 beds in use. Compared with these earlier methods, our approach is on a par with the best methods available today, or better, on our particular set of data.

One of the most important strengths of our model is that it is robust, meaning it stays reliable in several ways. First, we trained it, tuned it and checked it on a fairly large set of data. Second, we searched for the best settings in a systematic way. Settings close to the best ones seem to make only a fairly small difference to the results.

Another sign of stability is how much the errors differ between the data the model learned from (the training data) and the data we held back to check it (the validation data). Here the difference is small. The MAPE was 5.48% on the training data and 6.24% on the validation data. The mean absolute error (MAE), which is the average size of the error in beds rather than as a percentage, was 12.10 on the training data and 12.51 on the validation data. This shows that the model was not overfitting, which means it was not simply memorising the training data instead of learning general patterns. One reason is that, at each step, we built and averaged 50 models (N = 50), and each model is small.

Using several different error measures gives us better control over the tuning. We used the mean absolute error (MAE) to guide the tuning, because it shows how good the model is over the whole forecast period. In most cases, the other measures we used, MAPE, MAX (the largest error) and RMSE, follow the MAE. The last measure, the group error (GE), is harder to understand. It does not depend directly on the day-to-day differences between the predicted and the forecast number of beds. A difference of just one bed can mean that the number of bed groups needed is different. We still report this error because it matters for hospital planning.

Overall, the results of our tests are acceptable, and they encourage using our model as part of a hospital planning system.

Finally, although we tuned the model for 60 days of the summer season, it also works well for forecasts covering a whole year.

Perhaps the most surprising result of this paper is that our model predicts best using only information from the previous year, even though much longer records were available. This makes the calculations faster. It may also bring other advantages or disadvantages, which should be studied in future. For example, because the model looks back over a short period, it can adapt more quickly when the hospital changes, such as when a new ward opens or an old one closes.

On the other hand, the short look-back period also brings some limitations. One-off local events, such as disasters or outbreaks of disease, might not be predictable, and they could have a bigger effect on the following year. The same is true for events that happen less often, such as the Olympic Games or soccer championships. In a similar way, Jones [37] reported that the number of beds in use can switch on and off, rising quickly and then falling quickly, in a cycle that lasts 2 years. A model that looks back over less than one full cycle cannot capture this. Using several years of data can smooth out these swings and reduce the possible error in such cases. However, we did not see any on/off switching, or any other events with this kind of effect, in our work.

There are several ways to improve the model further. The most obvious is to improve the tuning process. Some settings in the model can still be adjusted. For example, we assumed that the delays in the internal data and in the outside information are the same. Dropping this assumption would be easy and would give us one more setting to adjust.

Another thing to consider is the weather, especially extreme heat or cold, as well as other outside factors such as flu outbreaks. Our forecasts cover 60 days, which is much longer than the detailed weather forecasts that can be trusted. For this reason, we decided not to include weather in the model. However, Bayesian modelling [38], a way of building models that also measure how uncertain they are, could help us take this kind of uncertainty into account.

When forecasts cover longer periods, other factors might matter. For instance, Jones [39] suggested that the number of deaths in a hospital could help predict how many beds will be in use.

Lastly, prediction intervals could also be a useful addition. A prediction interval is a range that shows how uncertain a prediction is, so it would let users see how much they can trust the model.
